title: Ethics of AI in Law: Basic Questions
pub: The Oxford Handbook of Ethics of AI (Oxford Univ. Press, 2020), ch. 38
author: Harry Surden

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal automation: Classification success cannot prove reasoning
st.an: The source provides a conceptual taxonomy of legal AI, distinguishing task automation from underlying technologies and identifying machine-learning and rules-based families. It does not compare classification with legal reasoning or assess whether success on bounded tasks demonstrates general legal competence, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: If we use technology to fully or partially automate these legal tasks, it                   is common to consider this a use of “artificial intelligence” within law.

The first                   group of AI technologies is broadly known as “machine learning,” and the second cate-                   gory is referred to as “knowledge representation and rules-based AI”.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s emphasis on reliable, accountable deployment rather than accuracy alone, and materially extends it to judicial decision support by identifying interpretability, reason-giving and habitual deference as risks that formal human discretion may not resolve. Its claims are conceptual and predictive rather than empirical.
qs: Thus,                   to the extent that government-aided AI decisions are made using machine learning                   techniques that are relatively less interpretable, we may be concerned that the value of                   transparency in decision-making is diminished.

If an AI-based system produces an automated risk assessment that has the aura of                   mathematical precision and objectivity, there are reasons to suspect that judges might                   opt to routinely adopt the automated recommendations by default even if they nomi-                   nally retain the final discretion to come to a different conclusion.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Surden accepts the cluster’s premise that AI has limited, context-dependent capabilities and requires human and institutional judgment. He materially extends it by showing how design choices and deferential reliance can redistribute fairness, responsibility and accountability, making legal values and institutional context part of selective deployment and work redesign.
qs: Rather, as explained previously, most AI approaches               involve automated approximations—learning computer-based patterns, rules, or heu-               ristics that can sometimes be used to produce “intelligent results without intelligence” in               certain, limited settings.

If judges begin routinely adopting, by the default, the recommendation of the system,                   this results in subtle shift of responsibility and accountability away from the judge and                   toward the AI recommendation systems and their creators.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: The source supports retaining identifiable human accountability and recognises that judges may have contextual evidence unavailable to AI. Its conditional case for greater AI use if empirically more accurate qualifies—but does not reject—the cluster’s supervised-assistance model, because it does not advocate transferring final judicial authority.
qs: Only empirical research will show whose predictions are more accu-               rate.
There are, therefore, identifiable points of               accountability—when a decision occurs, we know which official actor or body—judge               or jury—made the decision.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source aligns with the synthesis’s balanced view: careful AI use may improve access and efficiency, while unequal access to superior tools could deepen existing resource disparities. Its claims are largely conditional and ethical rather than empirical, and it does not directly examine unrepresented users’ limited verification capacity.
qs: Careful uses of AI may actually reduce bias, expose existing injustices, or                   increase access to the legal system and overall efficiency.5 To the extent that AI is used to                   enhance values such as fairness, equality, or access to justice, the legal system, and soci-                   ety more broadly, may benefit.

While it is true today that lawyers and clients who have more                resources can often obtain better outcomes than less resourced clients despite the rela-                tive merits of their positions, it is possible that AI-based tools could exacerbate this                divide.

st.t: Legal prediction: Classification cannot guarantee sound advice
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s cautious separation of predictive performance from sound legal practice. It treats superior AI prediction as hypothetical, then identifies distinct professional-duty and access-to-justice consequences rather than assuming accuracy alone guarantees appropriate advice or fair outcomes.
qs: For the sake of argument, imagine that in the near future, the predictions of case out-                comes made by lawyers using AI systems begin to vastly outperform the predictions                made by traditional lawyers using only their professional skills.22 This future scenario                raises several issues.

While it is true today that lawyers and clients who have more                resources can often obtain better outcomes than less resourced clients despite the rela-                tive merits of their positions, it is possible that AI-based tools could exacerbate this                divide.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s core view that AI is entering discrete legal tasks without eliminating the continuing importance of professional judgment and human responsibility. It reinforces caution about uncritical reliance and unequal access, though its contribution is primarily ethical and hypothetical rather than empirical or operational, and it does not substantively address verification, training, or apprenticeship design.
qs: lawyers have begun to use AI systems in a number of settings that were traditionally in               the purview of legal judgment, including automated document analysis, automated               ­discovery, and in legal case outcome prediction.

The central ethical ­challenge                   is to identify the way in which the use of AI may be shifting core legal values and to                   ensure that these crucial values are preserved in the technological transition.

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: The source directly supports the proposition that predictive accuracy cannot by itself legitimate machine adjudication. It treats accountability, acceptable justification, opportunities to be heard and perceived fairness as independent requirements, while cautioning that AI should be compared with imperfect human decision-making rather than an idealised baseline.
qs: There are, therefore, identifiable points of               accountability—when a decision occurs, we know which official actor or body—judge               or jury—made the decision.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core insistence that AI should not displace professional or judicial judgment. It warns that routine judicial adoption of automated recommendations could transfer effective decision-making to private system designers and frames responsible adoption around preserving core legal values. It does not materially address tool-specific verification burdens, lifecycle confidentiality controls, or whether checking consumes efficiency gains.
qs: If indeed judges begin to routinely adopt automated recommendations without                   much additional consideration, the locus of the decision essentially shifts to the organi-                   zation that designed and implemented the AI system—these days, often private compa-                   nies.

The central ethical ­challenge                   is to identify the way in which the use of AI may be shifting core legal values and to                   ensure that these crucial values are preserved in the technological transition.

kp.k: Legal AI ethics concerns preserving core legal values
kp.d: Surden surveys AI within the US legal system, framing its central ethical challenge as preserving equality, due process, transparency, explanation, independent adjudication and access to justice. AI may strengthen or weaken these values or change their relative priority; perceived erosion of these norms may also undermine institutional legitimacy. This is a conceptual and normative survey rather than a new empirical study.
qs: As AI becomes               increasingly integrated within the legal system, how can society ensure that core legal               values are preserved?
Careful uses of AI may actually reduce bias, expose existing injustices, or                   increase access to the legal system and overall efficiency.

kp.k: Analysis must remain grounded in contemporary technical capabilities
kp.d: The chapter distinguishes machine learning, which learns patterns from data, from knowledge representation and rules-based systems, illustrated by tax-compliance software. Surden characterizes contemporary AI as limited automation rather than human-like intelligence. His opinion that strong AI was unlikely within five to ten years is explicitly time-bound to the chapter's writing, not an established finding or a present-day assessment.
qs: where relevant data is unavailable or limited, machine learning approaches generally               cannot be applied.

As of the writing of this chapter, it is this                   author’s opinion that there is little to no evidence that such strong AI technology will be                   coming any time soon in the five-to-ten-year time frame.

kp.k: Government AI carries distinctive consequences for public power
kp.d: Surden distinguishes administrators of law, legal practitioners and users of law. He concentrates on government administrators because their decisions carry state authority and sanctions. Criminal sentencing and bail risk assessment illustrate how machine-learning predictions enter official decisions; the chapter's simplified examples explain mechanisms rather than report observed results for particular defendants.
qs: They have the ability to officially interpret and apply the                   law and have the power of the state and its sanctions behind them.

Such software will typically output a report                   with an overall risk-score for each defendant (e.g., risk rating on a scale from 1 to 10) to                   assist the judge in her decision.
The scores are merely recommen-                   dations, and, in principle, a judge is free to disregard them.

kp.k: Historical data can reproduce and reinforce unequal treatment
kp.d: Using a hypothetical example, Surden explains how unequal police patrol, arrest and recording practices could make low-income defendants appear more likely to reoffend even when underlying offense rates are equal. A predictive system could learn those patterns and recommend unequal bail treatment. The mechanism concerns structural bias encoded in data, not an empirical estimate of discriminatory performance.
qs: existing societal or structural biases may be subtly embedded in data sets.

Worse yet, if widespread, such AI systems may not only encode existing                   structural or institutional biases but may inadvertently reinforce and strengthen those                   biases

kp.k: Model design embeds consequential human judgments
kp.d: Surden emphasizes that selecting datasets, variables, algorithms, validation criteria and final models involves subjective decisions. These choices may favor or disadvantage social groups, unintentionally or deliberately. The possibility of intentional manipulation is presented as a concern reported from scholarship, not as a documented incident.
qs: There are also judgments about how to validate and measure whether the model is               working “well” or accurately or fairly.
The designers of such systems, therefore, have a great deal of power.
Some design biases might be largely unintentional

kp.k: Evaluate AI against imperfect institutions, not idealized humans
kp.d: Surden argues that AI bias must be compared with existing judicial biases and institutional design choices. Carefully implemented systems might reveal existing injustice and improve consistency, but apparent mechanical neutrality can encourage unwarranted trust. He also cautions that public-defender funding and institutional reforms may improve equality more than marginal technological adjustments.
qs: what legal processes existed before the tech-               nology was introduced, and what biases are in the current system?
In some cases, people have a tendency to unjustifiably treat automated outcomes as unbiased and authoritative as compared to human-based decisions.
time and effort might be better spent providing more funding for                    public defenders

kp.k: Commercial secrecy and technical opacity obstruct transparency
kp.d: The chapter identifies distinct barriers to scrutinizing risk-assessment systems: private vendors may withhold models, code and training data through trade secrecy, nondisclosure agreements and technical obfuscation; complex models may remain difficult to interpret even when accessible. Surden connects these barriers to public notice, transparent legal criteria and meaningful appeal, while noting that interpretable systems could offer greater reconstructability than human reasoning.
qs: These companies often do not make               their AI models, or the underlying data or software necessary for reconstructing the               decision, accessible to the public.
This also can impact the ability to appeal such               decisions—another core legal value.
the human mind is not an observable system either.

kp.k: Computational explanation is not necessarily adequate legal justification
kp.d: Surden distinguishes tracing mathematical operations from giving socially and legally acceptable reasons for decisions affecting rights. He reports concerns that reliance on AI could undervalue adjudication's humanistic and performative dimensions, including parties' experience of being heard and treated fairly. Technical auditability therefore does not by itself satisfy the chapter's account of legitimate explanation.
qs: Officials often must explicitly justify them in                   writing using socially and legally acceptable reasons.
such an computational exposition does not amount to a socially acceptable                   justification or satisfactory explanation for a human defendant.

kp.k: Comparative predictive accuracy remains an empirical question
kp.d: Surden cites research on human probabilistic reasoning and computer prediction to suggest that carefully designed AI might outperform judges in predicting reoffending. Conversely, judges can consider testimony and contextual evidence unavailable to systems limited to encoded information. The chapter does not establish universal superiority for either approach; any ethical argument for wider AI use depends on demonstrated comparative accuracy.
qs: Much research shows that humans reason poorly when it comes to probability               due to various cognitive biases.
judges can take into account a wide range of holistic and testimonial               evidence in making a decision
Only empirical research will show whose predictions are more accu-               rate.

kp.k: Deference to scores can shift accountability toward vendors
kp.d: Surden warns that judges might reflexively adopt nominally advisory risk scores because of apparent mathematical authority and potential backlash from overriding a high score. Numerical ratings may conceal uncertainty and false precision. If routine deference develops, substantive responsibility could migrate from publicly accountable judges to systems and the private organizations that design them. This is a conditional institutional risk, not a measured finding about judicial behavior.
qs: Indeed, judges have incentives not                   to override automated recommendations.
such scores suffer from                   the problem of false precision.
Another related issue is the shift of accountability from the public sector to the private                   sector.

kp.k: AI enters tasks traditionally dependent on lawyers' judgment
kp.d: The chapter describes lawyers beginning to use AI for document analysis, discovery and case-outcome prediction. These applications overlap with professional judgments about likely legal outcomes and which documents are privileged, important or relevant. The source identifies task-level changes but does not supply adoption rates, staffing effects or quantified productivity gains.
qs: including automated document analysis, automated               ­discovery, and in legal case outcome prediction.
predicting which documents               will be privileged or important or relevant to litigation or business matters.

kp.k: Superior prediction could alter duties and widen resource disparities
kp.d: Surden explicitly hypothesizes a near future in which AI-assisted lawyers substantially outperform unaided lawyers at predicting outcomes. He asks whether professional standards would then require AI use, without asserting an existing obligation. He also warns that unequal access to better tools could amplify resource advantages and undermine access to justice and merits-based adjudication, while acknowledging that such inequalities already exist.
qs: This future scenario                raises several issues.
will the ethical or professional standards shift such that lawyers                are obligated to use such systems
it is possible that AI-based tools could exacerbate this                divide.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Surden describes existing task-specific legal automation and conditional changes to fairness, transparency, accuracy, accountability and professional practice, rather than predicting wholesale lawyer replacement.
pts.d: In this 2020 chapter, Surden describes machine learning being used for prediction, document examination and legal-context analysis, alongside rules-based systems such as tax-compliance software. He argues that AI can encode and reinforce existing structural biases through training data and subjective design choices, but can also expose previously unnoticed injustices and potentially increase consistency. He stresses comparison with existing human and institutional biases, rather than an idealised bias-free baseline. Private vendors' secrecy and technically uninterpretable models can diminish transparency, notice and the ability to appeal; computational explanations may also fail to supply socially acceptable reasons for legal decisions. Conversely, accessible, interpretable systems can make aspects of decision-making reconstructable. Carefully implemented predictive systems might improve risk predictions, but judges may outperform them where relevant testimony or contextual information cannot be encoded. Nominally advisory risk scores could become defaults through judicial deference, shifting practical responsibility from judges to systems and private designers. For practitioners, Surden explicitly posits a hypothetical future in which AI-assisted case predictions substantially outperform unaided lawyers: this raises a question about whether professional standards would require using such tools and a possibility that unequal access would exacerbate existing advantages for better-resourced lawyers and clients. These are conditional possibilities and ethical questions, not established performance findings or claims of an existing professional obligation.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The chapter offers a literature-based ethical analysis, illustrative mechanisms and hypothetical scenarios, not original quantitative tests of legal-AI performance.
pts.d: Surden supports the bias discussion with scholarship including Barocas and Selbst's 'Big Data’s Disparate Impact' and Kroll and colleagues' 'Accountable Algorithms'; the example of unequal police recording of otherwise equal offending rates is expressly hypothetical. His description of criminal risk-assessment tools cites ProPublica's 'Machine Bias' and EPIC. The transparency and explanation discussion references Selbst and Barocas, Kaminski, and Miller. The accuracy discussion cites Kleinberg and colleagues' 'Human Decisions and Machine Predictions', Kahneman on human cognitive biases, and Agrawal, Gans and Goldfarb on prediction, including experience outside law. The chapter reports no numerical comparative accuracy results and leaves comparative legal prediction performance to empirical research. Judicial deference and transfers of accountability are developed through incentive-based reasoning and an imagined high-risk-score scenario, not a reported measurement of judges' behaviour. The practitioner discussion references Katz's work on quantitative legal prediction, but its scenario of greatly superior AI-assisted predictions remains an assumption introduced for argument. Surden's near-term assessment of strong AI is explicitly his opinion, not a benchmark result.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Surden limits the analysis to contemporary and near-term AI as understood when writing the 2020 chapter, with effects contingent on implementation, data and institutional behaviour.
pts.d: Descriptions of present capabilities belong to the chapter's historical setting, not to present-day generative AI. Surden frames the chapter around current capabilities and a near-term horizon of five years; separately, he expresses doubt about evidence for strong AI arriving within five to ten years of writing. Machine-learning applicability depends on relevant data, and its judgments are limited to information encoded in data and selected by designers. Fairness and accuracy gains depend on careful construction, implementation and recognition of limitations. Improved transparency requires suitable access and interpretable techniques; vendor confidentiality and complex models may frustrate it. Accountability shifts depend on judges routinely adopting recommendations despite formally retaining discretion. Changes to lawyers' professional obligations and resource inequalities are conditional on the hypothetical superiority of AI-assisted predictions in the near future. Surden does not quantify adoption, market effects or employment consequences and warns that institutional design, funding, political power and other non-AI factors may matter more.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The central affected groups are legal administrators and people subject to state decisions; the practitioner discussion concerns lawyers and clients with unequal access to predictive tools.
pts.d: Surden distinguishes administrators of law, practitioners, and users of law, giving most attention to administrators because they exercise state-backed authority. Judges and juries may gain predictive assistance while risking excessive deference and weakened accountability. Criminal defendants face consequences for bail, sentencing, explanation and appeal; disadvantaged groups may bear amplified historical or design biases, though carefully implemented systems could also improve their treatment. Private software vendors and designers may acquire practical influence over public legal judgments; they are described as suppliers of technology, not alternative legal service providers delivering legal work. Lawyers may acquire stronger prediction and document-analysis capabilities, while better-resourced lawyers and clients could gain additional advantages over those without equivalent tools. Ordinary citizens and businesses are identified as users of law, with tax-compliance software illustrating rules-based assistance. The public has a stake in equality, access to justice and institutional legitimacy. The chapter does not distinguish effects by law-firm size, staffing structure, billing model or specific legal-market segment.
